1.pericope_label: The league of the five kings against Gibeon

schools.summary: Gill takes the name of Jerusalem for the possession of Salem, records the Jewish scruple about its spelling and the rival senses others have given the name, and gives the distances of Gibeon and Hebron from the city on the authority of Josephus and Jerome. He explains that the five are called Amorites because that people, though the men of Jerusalem were Jebusites and those of Hebron Hittites, were the most powerful in the land and dispersed through every part of it, so that the name covered the rest. Calvin explains the shape of the narrative, that what had been glanced at before is now told at length and that what was said of the kings in general is applied to one man, not because Adoni-zedek alone was afraid but because he stirred up all the others and was the chief author and leader of the war, the plural verb showing that all were of one mind while some hung back from fear. He adds the reasoning behind the choice of target, that they turned first upon Gibeon both to make an example of men who had betrayed their country and to give their own soldiers confidence by terrifying a beaten enemy, having a fair pretext in punishing those who had preferred to sanction strangers rather than defend their neighbours.

Henry begins with the delay rather than the alarm, since Israel had been a good while in Canaan with no great matters effected, Jericho taken by a miracle, Ai by stratagem and Gibeon by surrender, so that Joshua’s prudence was perhaps censured as slothfulness and want of spirit. He answers that Canaan was not to be conquered in a day, God having said he would drive out the nations by little and little, and he that believeth will not make haste; that Joshua waited for the Canaanites to be the aggressors so that their destruction might be the more justifiable before men as well as God, and they the more inexcusable after seeing the favour the Gibeonites found; and that it was to Israel’s advantage for the little kings to combine into one body and be cut off at one blow, which God had in view when he put it into their hearts to confederate, since they meant to strengthen one another while he meant to gather them as sheaves into the floor. Of Adoni-zedek he supposes that he may have descended from Melchizedek, and remarks that for all the goodness of his name and family he was a bad man and an implacable enemy of the posterity of that Abraham to whom his predecessor had been so faithful a friend.

Clarke sets out the whole campaign in summary before turning to the towns, giving the distance of each from Jerusalem and the later fortunes of Lachish, where Amaziah was slain by conspirators and which was besieged by Sennacherib without effect and afterwards by the army of Nebuchadnezzar. He denies that Gibeon was a royal city in the strict sense and makes it a small but powerful republic governed by its elders, since no king of the Gibeonites is anywhere mentioned and their own embassy to Joshua named none; and he explains the name Amorite as a general term for the inhabitants of Canaan, the men of Jerusalem being Jebusites, those of Hebron Hittites and the Gibeonites Hivites. Wesley agrees that Adoni-zedek sent either because he was superior to the others or because he was nearest the danger and most forward in the work, allows either that Gibeon was really a royal city or merely equal to one though governed by elders, and supposes that the Amorites, being numerous and victorious beyond Jordan, poured colonies into Canaan and so communicated their name to the rest.

Ellicott sets Lord of Righteousness beside King of Righteousness and finds the likeness of the names good evidence that the Salem of Genesis was Jerusalem, adding that the title may have belonged to its king not only as a local style but in relation to the surrounding tribes over whom he may have been suzerain, though we know nothing of the matter beyond the sacred text. He identifies the confederate towns so far as they can be identified while admitting that Lachish is still uncertain, takes the phrase about Gibeon to mean one of the cities of the kingdom and notes that it was afterwards the city of Saul, and observes the striking fact that in all the wars of Canaan we never read of one direct attack upon Joshua and his army, the Canaanites acting strictly on the defensive and every army that took the field being attacked before it ventured to attack him. Keil and Delitzsch carry the later history of Jerusalem forward, allotted to Benjamin but situated on the border of Judah, conquered and burnt by the sons of Judah after Joshua’s death, soon retaken and rebuilt by the Jebusites whom Judah could not destroy, so that both tribes lived there alongside them and the upper town upon Zion remained a Jebusite fortress until David took it and called it by his own name.

debates: What standing Gibeon had: Clarke denies it was a royal city in any strict sense and makes it a republic governed by elders, since no Gibeonite king is ever named, while Ellicott reads the phrase as one of the cities of the kingdom and points to Gibeon as the later city of Saul, and Wesley allows either that it was royal or merely equal to a royal city

Why Joshua had not moved sooner: Henry defends the delay as deliberate, since Canaan was not to be conquered in a day, the Canaanites had to strike first for the war to be manifestly just, and the scattered kings were better destroyed once they had gathered into one body
outliers: Ellicott observes that in all the wars of Canaan there is no record of a single direct attack upon Joshua, every Canaanite army that took the field being attacked before it attacked him
Clarke argues from the silence of the record about any Gibeonite king that the city was governed as a republic by its elders

6.pericope_label: The appeal of the Gibeonites, the march from Gilgal, and the divine assurance

schools.summary: Gill reports the opinion that the Gibeonites sent only when they were already besieged, which would show their faith in the God they now professed, but judges it unlikely both that they should defer so long, having heard of the muster at Jerusalem, and that they could get messengers out when surrounded on every side, and therefore renders the verb as a pluperfect, they had sent; he notes that Joshua went up because Gilgal lay low in the plains of Jericho, and that it is highly probable he consulted the Lord before setting out, having some doubt whether he was bound to assist men whose league had been obtained by fraud. Calvin says the same of the embassy more shortly, that the course of the narrative is inverted since the Gibeonites did not wait to be besieged but, seeing an army levied and having no doubt that they would sustain the first onset as the most hated of all, anticipated the attack and hastened to Joshua’s protection. On the oracle he says plainly that it is uncertain whether the Lord anticipated the movement and drew Joshua out of Gilgal before he had taken a step, or only confirmed him once his preparations were made, and thinks it likelier that Joshua did not rush forth without consulting God, since, having lately been chastised for excessive facility, he probably attempted nothing in this difficulty except by a divine command; and he adds that the Lord had respect to the wretched Gibeonites in not allowing them to remain destitute of the help of his people, making Joshua confident of victory precisely in order that he might succour them.

Henry makes the march an act of plain honesty. Joshua resolved to assist his new allies, which was generous and just, though the king of Jerusalem, who spoke so confidently of smiting Gibeon, had probably expected him to abandon them as Canaanites, and the rather because their league had been obtained by fraud; but Joshua knew that his promise to let them live obliged him not only not to slay them himself but not to stand by and see them slain when it was in the power of his hand to prevent it.

Wesley draws out the ground of the appeal in three parts, that Joshua was bound to protect the Gibeonites in duty as their master, by his own interest since they were now part of his possessions, and in ingenuity, because they had given themselves to him and put themselves under his protection. He holds that Joshua had asked advice of God before he went up, which the form of the answer implies, and takes the mighty men for an army of the most valiant picked out from the rest, since it is not probable either that he would take so many hundred thousand with him, who would only have hindered one another, or that he would leave the camp without an army to defend it.

Keil and Delitzsch gloss the plea itself, that to slack the hand from a servant is to withhold help from him, and warn that the clause about the Amorites who dwelt in the mountains is added of the chief part only, so that it does not warrant the conclusion that all the towns named were in the mountains of Judah, those mountain Amorites being the strongest of all the Canaanites; they note that the verb of Joshua’s setting out is ascended rather than went, that the men of valour are named by way of explanation rather than as a second body, and that the assurance given here is a renewal of earlier promises, this being the first time Joshua was to fight several allied kings of Canaan at once. Ellicott places the mountain Amorites in the hill country south of Jerusalem, and stands apart from the conjectures about the oracle by stating the pattern instead, that a distinct command is given for the beginning of this attack as for all the important steps in the conquest of Canaan.

debates: Whether the Gibeonites sent before the siege or during it: Gill records the view that they sent only when besieged, which would argue faith, but rejects it both because they had warning enough and because messengers could not have passed a surrounding army, and renders the verb as a pluperfect; Calvin agrees that the narrative is inverted and the embassy went out as soon as the muster was seen

Whether Joshua consulted God before setting out: Calvin leaves it formally uncertain while judging it likelier that he asked first, having lately been chastised for acting too readily, Gill and Wesley agree that he consulted, and Ellicott declines the conjecture and points instead to the regular pattern of a distinct command at every important step
outliers: Wesley grounds Joshua’s obligation to the Gibeonites in three things at once, duty as their master, interest as their owner, and ingenuity because they had given themselves to him
Keil and Delitzsch warn that the description of the Amorites as dwelling in the mountains is given of the chief part only and cannot be pressed to locate all five cities

9.pericope_label: The night march, the rout at Gibeon, and the great stones from heaven

schools.summary: Gill says that the suddenness of the attack threw the kings into consternation and confusion, and that they were troubled and frightened at the unexpected appearance of Israel; he describes the descent of Beth-horon toward Azekah as a very narrow passage of which Josephus makes mention, and reports the Jewish tradition that this was the place where the army of Sennacherib fell. Calvin uses the two slaughters to settle a question of agency: in the first the Lord exerted his own might but used the swords of the people, from which we infer that when he works by men nothing is detracted from his glory, since he does not call in allies as a subsidiary force or borrow anything from them, but, being able to accomplish whatever he pleases by a mere nod, uses men as instruments to show that they are ruled by his hand and will, so that it is equally true to say that the enemy were routed by God or by the Israelites; in the second the hand of God appeared more clearly, and the text states expressly that more died by the hail than by the sword, that no doubt might remain.

Clarke calls it a forced march by night over the eighteen or twenty miles from Gilgal to Gibeon, has multitudes falling in the first onset before the rest fled, notes that there were two cities called Beth-horon, upper and lower, both in the tribe of Ephraim and built by Sherah the daughter of Ephraim, though their exact situation is not known, and places Azekah and Makkedah in Judah. On the stones he reports the contention that common stones are meant and that the word hail marks only the speed and quantity of their fall, grants freely that stones have fallen from the clouds in the East Indies, America, France, Germany, England and Ireland, that he possesses fragments of such stones himself and that considerable pieces may be seen in the British Museum, and that God, whose power is unlimited, might certainly have cast such stones down, yet judges it more likely that hailstones in the proper sense are intended. Wesley observes that though assured by God of the victory Joshua uses all prudent means, and that it is not said he covered the ground in a night’s space but only that he travelled all night, since God’s promises are intended not to slacken but to quicken our endeavours, and he that believeth does not make haste to anticipate providence but does make haste to attend it, with a diligent and not a distrustful speed; he takes the stones for hailstones of extraordinary greatness, cast down with such certainty as to hit the Canaanites and not their pursuers, adds from Josephus that thunder and lightning were mixed with the hail, and closes on the irony that men who had robbed the true God of his honour by worshipping the host of heaven were now destroyed by the hosts of heaven, fleeing north and south alike with the hail pursuing them either way.

Ellicott corrects the rendering, since the sense is that Joshua came upon them suddenly because all the night he had been marching up from Gilgal, and observes that the verb of ascent is geographically exact, the line of march from Gilgal to Gibeon being an ascent the whole way. Keil and Delitzsch reckon the distance at fully fifteen miles and hold that the whole of it was accomplished in a night, take the confusion as the fulfilment of the promise given in Exodus and judge from what follows that it was produced by dreadful thunder and lightning, and trace the pursuit by the ascent of Upper Beth-horon, nearest to Gibeon, four hours off to the north-west on a lofty promontory between two valleys and divided from the lower town by a long steep pass. The great stones they take for hailstones rather than a shower of stones, a terrible storm in which the hail fell in pieces as large as stones and killed more than the swords of Israel, resembling the plague of hail in Egypt and manifestly miraculous, since the stones slew the enemy without injuring the Israelites who pursued them.

debates: What the great stones were: Clarke reports and takes seriously the contention that literal stones fell from the sky, citing recorded falls in several countries and specimens in the British Museum, but concludes for hail in the proper sense, while Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley take them as hailstones of extraordinary size and rest the miracle on their striking the Canaanites without touching the pursuers

How divine and human agency divide in the victory: Calvin makes the first slaughter God’s own work carried out by Israel’s swords, so that either description is true, while Keil and Delitzsch read even the initial confusion as produced directly by thunder and lightning
outliers: Clarke supports the possibility of a fall of literal stones from his own collection of fragments and from specimens then in the British Museum
Gill records the Jewish tradition that the descent of Beth-horon was the place where the army of Sennacherib afterwards fell
Wesley turns the hail into a reckoning, since those who had worshipped the host of heaven were destroyed by the hosts of heaven

12.pericope_label: Joshua commands the sun and moon, and the day is lengthened

schools.summary: Gill reads the first clause as prayer, Joshua entreating that sun and moon might stand still until the victory was complete, and records that the Jewish writers make it a song instead, the Targum having that Joshua then praised or sang praise, a reading which Jarchi and Kimchi approve; he marks the arrest itself, the sun that came out of his chamber like a bridegroom and rejoiced as a strong man to run his course stopping at once, and the moon that walks in her brightness going no further, both standing motionless. Calvin meets the difficulty of the address head on: some take the words to mean that Joshua spoke of Jehovah rather than to him, since addressing God, who ought rather to be suppliantly petitioned, seems little in accordance with the modesty of faith, and the next clause has him speaking to the sun; Calvin has no doubt that the first clause denotes a prayer or vow and the second an expression of confidence after he had been heard, for to command the sun without leave already obtained would have been presumptuous and arrogant, so that he consults God first and, having his answer, boldly commands the sun to do what he knows is pleasing to God. Such is the power of the faith Christ inspires that mountains and seas are moved at its command, and the more the godly feel their own emptiness the more liberally does God transfer his power to them, since faith borrows the confidence of command from the word on which it rests. He also refuses the whole enquiry into the manner of the miracle, holding that the question how the sun stood over Gibeon is as unseasonably raised by some as it is unskilfully explained by others, and that the rebuke falls with double force upon those who explain the miracle away, among whom are some of the most distinguished Jewish rabbis, who allow no miracle but only something very like one, chiefly out of zeal for the honour of Moses, whose reputation they think would suffer if his successor performed a wonder he never wrought. Joshua, he adds, did not subtly fix the sun in a point, so that there is no need to feign a battle fought at the summer solstice: as it was turning toward the district of Ajalon so far as the eye could reach, he bids it stay and rest above the horizon, and the sun, already declining westward, is kept from setting.

Clarke sets out his method before his explanation, taking it for granted that a miracle was wrought as nearly as circumstances admit in the manner recorded and refusing to look for any allegorical or metaphorical sense; he holds the received system of the universe to be genuine and also to be the system laid down in the Mosaic writings, with the sun at rest in the centre and the earth turning both about him and about its own axis in a little less than a full day, so that what we call the rising and setting of the sun is caused by the motion of the earth and not of the sun, as a ball hung before a candle will show; and he holds the solar influence to be the cause of both motions, alterable by no power but the unlimited power of God, who is nevertheless so free an agent that he can alter, suspend or even annihilate all secondary causes and their effects. Wesley has Joshua moved to the request by zeal against God’s enemies and by the motion of God’s Spirit, speaking before the people so that they might be witnesses; he denies that the two places are meant to fix the two lights, as though the sun stood over one and the moon over the other, which is absurd when the places lie so near together, and makes the doubling partly a poetical variation and partly a note of the line of pursuit from Gibeon toward Ajalon, the moon being asked to stay not because her light was needed but that the order of the heavens might not be broken. He takes the book of Jasher for a work written and published before Joshua wrote and therefore fitly cited here, now lost because it was not canonical and so not preserved by the Jews with the same care; answers the objection that no heathen writer records so wonderful a work by pointing out that the generality of writers admit there is no certain history or monument of anything done before the Trojan war, a thousand years after Joshua’s time, all before which the most learned heathens themselves call the uncertain or obscure time; and takes the whole day for an artificial day between sunrise and sunset, that being the day Joshua needed for his work.

Keil and Delitzsch hold that in firm reliance on the promise already given Joshua offered a prayer during the battle that the Lord would not let the sun go down till Israel had taken vengeance on their foes, and that the Lord hearkened to the prayer of his servant, so that the sun hasted not to go down till the defeat of the Amorites was accomplished; the victory was afterwards celebrated in a war-song preserved in the book of the Righteous, and it is generally admitted that these verses are a quotation from that book, introduced by the author of Joshua for the glorification of the name of the Lord upon Israel. Ellicott gives the words their literal force, that the sun was silent and the moon stopped, notes that the phrase rendered the midst of heaven means literally the half of the heavens and may equally mean the same hemisphere, and observes that the verb of going down cannot mean to rise or ascend, which absolutely excludes the view that what Joshua desired was to prevent the sun from rising in order to complete a night attack upon the Amorites.

debates: What Joshua actually did, and to whom he spoke: Gill records the Jewish reading which makes the first clause a song of praise rather than a prayer, Calvin distinguishes a petition first and a command afterwards and holds that commanding the sun without leave already obtained would have been presumptuous, and Wesley makes the whole a public act performed before witnesses

How far the miracle may be explained: Clarke insists on the fact and builds an astronomical framework around it while granting that only God can suspend the secondary causes he established, Calvin rebukes both those who raise the question and, with double force, those who explain the wonder away, and Ellicott settles one proposed reading on purely lexical grounds
outliers: Wesley answers the silence of the heathen historians by observing that no certain record of anything survives from before the Trojan war, which was a thousand years after Joshua
Calvin reports that the rabbis who reduced the miracle to something merely like one did so out of zeal for the honour of Moses, lest his successor should be found to have wrought what he never did
Ellicott renders the Hebrew literally as the sun was silent, and the moon stopped

14.pericope_label: No day like that: the singularity of the miracle, and the return to Gilgal

schools.summary: Gill guards the claim against two objections, that the comparison is not with natural days such as the long days of the polar regions but with miraculous ones, and that Hezekiah’s day cannot rival it, since it is uncertain whether the ten degrees of the shadow were hours or halves or quarters, and even if hours the return could add only ten and so make a day of twenty-two; besides which the writer speaks only of days that had been in his own time, and the point is less the length of the day than the manner of it. On the return to Gilgal he alone offers a defence of the order as it stands, that Joshua determined upon the return and prepared for it but was prevented by the news that the five kings were hidden in a cave at Makkedah, though he allows the alternative that the verse is out of its proper place or superfluous, since the same thing is said later and the Septuagint leaves it out. Calvin allows the Hezekiah parallel more room, since the course of the sun was afterwards changed as a favour to that king, so that it is not absolutely denied that anything similar was ever conceded to another, but the miracle is extolled as singular. He rejects as too harsh the rendering which makes the verb of hearkening mean that God obeyed, for though the Psalm says the Lord does according to the desire of his servants, which might be held equivalent, it is better to avoid anything that seems to give a subordinate office to God; and he holds that the verse about the return is not inserted in its proper place and is altogether omitted by the Septuagint, since what follows is the end of the battle, the punishment of the kings and the encampment at Makkedah, after which the return to Gilgal is repeated at the close of the chapter.

Henry reads the moment as a lesson in unfinished work. The five kings had made a brave appearance when they took the field for the reducing of Gibeon, and were now routed and destroyed by the hailstones, so that Joshua thought his work done and his army entitled to quarters of refreshment, and it was resolved, perhaps in a council of war, that they should return to the camp at Gilgal until they should receive orders from God to take possession of the country they had conquered; but he soon found he had more work cut out for him, since the victory had to be pursued if the spoils were to be divided, and he applied himself to it with renewed vigour, following and smiting the forces that had dispersed themselves and setting a guard over the kings for the present, reserving them for another day of destruction.

Clarke says simply that there was no period of time in which the sun was kept so long above the horizon, and reports that some learned men have supposed the fable of Phaeton to be founded on this historic fact, which may be read with all the elegance of poetic embellishment at the opening of the second book of Ovid, though he confesses he can see nothing in the pretended copy to justify the opinion. On the return he argues from the rest of the chapter that the army did not go back until after the hanging of the five kings and the destruction of their cities, notes that the verse is omitted by the Septuagint and the Anglo-Saxon and does not appear to have existed in the ancient hexaplar versions, judges that it is not merely useless where it stands but an encumbrance to the narrative since it stands properly at the close of the chapter, and proposes, if it is genuine here, to read Makkedah for Gilgal, Joshua having a temporary camp there. Wesley answers the objection from the polar days by observing that those are long by the order of nature while this length was purely contingent and granted in answer to Joshua’s prayer, presses the sense of the hearkening without the disputed word, that God altered the course of nature and of the heavenly bodies so that a man might have more time to destroy his enemies, takes the clause about the Lord fighting for Israel as the reason of that readiness, and adds that the wonder was designed for more than light to finish a battle by, being meant to convince and confound the idolaters who worshipped the sun and moon by showing that these too were subject to the command of the God of Israel; on the return he agrees that it was not upon the same day but after the matters that follow, the very same words being repeated later, and takes the sentence as closing the general account of the fight before the particular passages are described.

Ellicott holds that the words about there being no day like that are meaningless unless the writer intended to convey the idea that there was really a great miracle, and compares the prophecy of Isaiah that the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun and the light of the sun sevenfold in the day when the Lord binds up the breach of his people; the verse about the return to Gilgal he calls a relation by anticipation in the words of the Book of Jasher of what is narrated at the close of the chapter, since the immediate return at the end of the miraculous day’s operations was to Makkedah and not to Gilgal.

debates: Whether the verse about the return stands in its place: Clarke, Calvin, Ellicott and Wesley all treat it as anticipation or misplacement, Clarke adding the versional evidence and proposing to read Makkedah for Gilgal, while Gill alone defends the order by supposing that Joshua really intended to return and was prevented by the news of the hidden kings

How this day compares with the day of Hezekiah: Gill computes that the retreating shadow could have added at most ten hours and so made a shorter day, Calvin declines to deny that something similar was ever conceded to another and calls the miracle singular rather than unrepeatable, and Ellicott rests the whole force of the words on the reality of the wonder
outliers: Clarke reports and then dismisses the suggestion that the fable of Phaeton in Ovid was founded on this history
Calvin refuses to let the verb be rendered as though God obeyed a man, holding it better to avoid every phrase that seems to give God a subordinate office
Wesley makes the arrest of the sun and moon a direct rebuke to those who worshipped them, since it showed both to be subject to the God of Israel

16.pericope_label: The five kings hidden in the cave, the pursuit pressed home, and the return in peace

schools.summary: Gill marks the escape of the five as itself providential, since they were neither killed by the hailstones nor slain by the sword of Israel but made their escape, being reserved by the providence of God for a more shameful end; he supposes the news of their hiding was brought to Joshua either by some of his own people or by inhabitants of the land who were in his interest, has the stones rolled up to keep the kings in until Joshua should have convenient time to bring them out and deal with them as they deserved, remarking that there was no doubt plenty of stone about the hill fit for the purpose, and takes the phrase of the return for sound and well, not one killed or missing and, as the Latin has it, not one wounded either, the army coming back in full number. Calvin faces the harder question raised by what follows: the enemy being completely routed, Joshua is now free and at leisure to inflict punishment on the kings, but in considering this the divine command must always be kept in view, since without it there would be boundless arrogance and barbarous atrocity in trampling on the necks of kings and hanging their dead bodies upon gibbets. It is certain that they had lately been raised by divine agency to a sacred dignity and placed upon a royal throne, so that it would have been contrary to the feelings of humanity to exult in their ignominy had not God so ordered it; but since such was his pleasure it behoves us to acquiesce in his decision without presuming to inquire why he willed it so.

Clarke thinks it very likely that the cave was a fortified place among rocks, of which there were many in different parts of Palestine. The clause about the tongue he refers to Israel, holding that the whole transaction of that great day had been carried on so evidently under the direction of God that there was not the least murmuring among them, nor any cause for it, their enemies being wholly discomfited, and he compares a like expression in Exodus. Wesley calls the cave a place of the greatest secrecy and adds that there is no escaping the eye or the hand of God, observing that the town itself was not yet taken so that the hiding-place lay in its territory rather than in the city; he explains why the fugitives had to be kept from their cities, since men once inside them would recover their strength and renew the war, and reads the assurance that God has delivered them as meaning that the work will be easy, God having already done it to their hands. The clause about the tongue he refers instead to the Canaanites, finding in it that their men of war could not find their hands and were besides so confounded that they could not move their tongues by way of insult, as they doubtless did when Israel was smitten at Ai, so that now they were silenced as well as conquered and durst provoke the Israelites no more.

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew has the definite article, the cave in Makkedah, stops over the rare verb for smiting the hindmost, which occurs only once elsewhere in the Old Testament, and takes the occasion to observe that the command given to Israel to exterminate the Canaanites, perfectly general as it sounds, is nevertheless limited as to time and circumstances by the very condition attached to it in the giving, since Israel was to smite and utterly destroy the nations which the Lord should first bring them in against and cast out before them. Keil and Delitzsch summarise the outcome, that when the great battle and the pursuit of the enemy were ended and the enemy consumed with a very great slaughter, the remnant that remained of them entered into fenced cities.

debates: Whose tongue is meant in the closing clause: Clarke refers it to Israel and finds in it that there was not the least murmuring among them, since the day had so plainly been carried on under God’s direction, while Wesley refers it to the Canaanites, who could neither find their hands nor move their tongues to insult as they had done after Ai

On what footing the kings could be so treated: Calvin insists that trampling on royal necks and hanging the bodies would be boundless arrogance and barbarous atrocity but for the express command of God, whose pleasure must be acquiesced in without inquiry, while Ellicott observes that even the general command to exterminate the Canaanites is bounded by the conditions under which it was given
outliers: Clarke suggests that the cave was no mere hollow but a fortified place among the rocks, of a kind common in Palestine
Wesley contrasts the silence of the beaten Canaanites with the insults they had offered when Israel was repulsed at Ai

22.pericope_label: The kings brought out of the cave, the feet upon their necks, and their bodies hanged

schools.summary: Gill glosses the order simply, that the mouth of the cave was opened by rolling away the great stones laid against it and that the five were set before Joshua after he had passed sentence on them; the charge not to fear he takes as spoken not about the kings, who lay bound upon the ground and were in no condition to resist, but about the enemies still to be met, who would be brought into the same subjection and from whom the people should therefore take heart; and he notes that sunset was the time fixed by the law of God for taking down bodies that had been hanged. Calvin takes the act as a triumph in the persons of the five over all the rest who remained, since Joshua exhorts his own people to confidence just as if those who still stood unsubdued were already prostrate beneath their feet; by the trampling down of a few the whole people were so elated that they looked with contempt upon all the others as if already overthrown, and in that we have a brighter display of the divine power, which could thus inspire confidence for the future. He adds that the kings were hung up, not for the purpose of exercising greater severity upon them.

Clarke calls the setting of feet on the necks symbolic, a token not only of the present complete victory but of the approaching triumph over all their adversaries, which is the interpretation Joshua himself gives in the following verse. On the hanging he is careful to clear the practice: hanging alive seems a barbarous custom, but among the Hebrews criminals were first deprived of life, which was the debt required by justice, and only then hanged up, perhaps generally by the hands rather than by the neck, by way of example to deter others from the crimes for which they had suffered; and they were never permitted to hang all night, since that could answer no purpose either of justice or of example, the bodies not being visible in the night season, one day being deemed enough to show the public that justice had been done. Wesley denies that the act was done out of pride or contempt and makes it a punishment of impious rebellion against their sovereign Lord, in pursuance of the curse of servitude due to all that people, and a token to assure the captains that God would subdue the proudest of them under their feet; the bodies, he says, were taken down so that neither wild beasts could come to devour them nor any of their own people give them honourable burial, and he closes on the shape of the whole episode, that what they thought would be their shelter was made their prison first and then their grave, so that we shall surely be disappointed in whatever we flee to from God.

Ellicott stops over the word for the captains, which occurs here for the first time and seems to mean the actual leaders rather than merely the official heads of the people, the men who had borne the brunt of the battle, and who, having laboured, deserved to see the fruit of their labour, the act being well calculated to inspirit them and to fire them with courage to lead their followers in the battles still to come; he observes that the words of encouragement are the very words Jehovah had spoken to Joshua at the outset except that the term for fear is the stronger one there, so that even ordinary fear is needless and alarm not to be thought of, and he takes the hanging here as a token of disgrace after death, turning it forward to the cross of the true Joshua, upon which the enemies of the Israel of God are exhibited and a show made of them openly. Keil and Delitzsch name the five kings by their cities and set out the sequence, that Joshua called for all the men of Israel, directed the leaders of the army to set their feet upon the necks of the kings, and only then had them put to death and hanged upon trees until the evening, their bodies being thrown at last into the cave in which they had concealed themselves.

debates: What the foot upon the neck signified: Clarke makes it a symbol of the triumph still to come, Wesley a judicial punishment of rebellion and a pledge given to the captains, Calvin a means by which the whole people were elated to contempt of the enemies still standing, and Ellicott an act calculated to inspirit the very men who had borne the brunt of the fighting

How the hanging is to be understood: Clarke insists that the men were dead before they were hung and explains the custom and its one-day limit, Ellicott takes it as a token of disgrace after death and reads it forward to the cross, and Calvin denies that it was meant as any aggravation of severity
outliers: Ellicott sees in the exposure of the five kings a figure of the cross of the true Joshua, where the enemies of the Israel of God are made a show of openly
Clarke suggests that the Hebrews hanged their dead criminals by the hands rather than by the neck
Wesley points out that the cave was in turn the shelter, the prison and the grave of the men who fled to it

28.pericope_label: Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish and the king of Gezer

schools.summary: Gill refers the phrase about that day more narrowly to the day on which the five kings were hanged, while noting that some make it the day the sun stood still; he gives the distances between the towns on Bunting’s authority, notes that the second day of the siege of Lachish may be reckoned either from the slaughter of the kings or, as Kimchi has it, from the beginning of the encampment, and supposes that Horam of Gezer was the readier to come up because Lachish had no king of its own to defend it, observing that whether he arrived before the city fell or after he was either unable to raise the siege or too late, and in both cases fell into Joshua’s hands. Calvin measures the conquest by its difficulty: here are the cities out of which the enemy’s army had been raised, and in taking them God displayed his power no less wonderfully than in the open field, especially when the rapidity is considered, for the men who fled into them might at first spread panic, but once the fear was allayed they could serve for defence, the garrisons having been increased by their numbers.

Henry stands back and praises the generalship, since Joshua improved the victory he had won and the advantages it gave him, and to do this well is a general’s praise. Of the cities of the five kings he went and took possession of Lachish, Eglon and Hebron, though Jerusalem and Jarmuth were not taken at this time, his forces being perhaps too fatigued with what they had done or too well content with what they had gained.

Clarke allows the long day the first town only: it is very possible that Makkedah was taken on the evening of the same day as the miraculous solstice, but the other cities mentioned in the chapter were certainly subdued some days later, since an army exhausted by a whole night’s march and two days’ hard fighting could not possibly have proceeded further that night, the rest being taken successively on the following days. He sets Libnah near Makkedah and adds that Sennacherib besieged it after being obliged to raise the siege of Lachish, observes that Lachish was anciently a very strong place since for all the panic of the enemy and the success of Israel Joshua could not reduce it until the second day, and thinks Horam of Gezer was in alliance with the king of Lachish and came to his assistance as soon as it appeared he would be attacked, Joshua probably sending a detachment against him before he could effect a junction. Wesley takes the whole run of the conquests as belonging to the long day, and finds nothing strange in so much work being done and places so far distant being taken in one day, when the day was so long and the Canaanites struck with such terror.

Ellicott suggests a pluperfect, that Joshua had taken Makkedah before the execution of the five kings, prefers a simple conjunction to the adverb at the opening of the next stage, treats the operations against Libnah as the commencement of a further stage of the campaign while admitting that the site has not been identified, lists the rival identifications of Lachish while allowing that it cannot have been far from Eglon, and connects the two days of that siege with two later facts, that Sennacherib laid siege to Lachish with all his power and had to abandon it, and that Jeremiah names Lachish and Azekah among the defenced cities of Judah that were left when Nebuchadnezzar invaded; Gezer he identifies a few miles from Emmaus. Keil and Delitzsch date the capture of Makkedah to the day of the impaling and describe the terms, the town and its king smitten with the edge of the sword, the inhabitants put to death under the ban, the cattle and property taken as booty as in the case of Ai, and the king treated as the king of Jericho had been; Libnah they place among the towns of the plain or hill country of Judah, allotted to the priests, in revolt from Judah under Joram and besieged by Sennacherib, and look for it to the north-west of Lachish; and they note that nothing is said about the capture of the town of Gezer itself, which by later notices remained in Canaanite possession.

debates: How much of the campaign belongs to the long day: Wesley takes the whole run of conquests to have followed within it, Gill refers the phrase to the day of the executions, Clarke allows only Makkedah and argues from the exhaustion of an army that had marched all night and fought two days, and Ellicott proposes reading the verb as a pluperfect

Whether the flight of the beaten army helped or hindered the towns: Calvin observes that the fugitives might spread panic at first but could serve for defence once their fear was allayed, and that the garrisons were in fact increased by them, which makes the speed of the captures the more wonderful
outliers: Ellicott ties the two-day resistance of Lachish to its later history, when Sennacherib had to abandon the siege of it and Jeremiah still counted it among the defenced cities left standing
Keil and Delitzsch point out that the capture of Gezer itself is never recorded, and that it remained in Canaanite hands long afterwards

34.pericope_label: Eglon, Hebron and Debir taken, and the king of Hebron

schools.summary: Gill puts Eglon at eight miles from Lachish and twelve from Jerusalem to the south on Bunting’s reckoning, notes that the town fell on the same day the army encamped and besieged it, the besieged finding themselves unable to hold it, and observes that Hebron lay in the hill country so that the army is said to go up to it from the lower ground of Eglon, sixteen miles away. Debir he takes for a city Joshua had passed by on his way to Hebron without fighting against it and returned to take once Hebron had fallen, reporting Bunting’s estimate of a mile from Hebron and twenty-two from Jerusalem southward, though he doubts that figure afterwards, since Debir was itself a royal city with others depending on it and must therefore have lain further off, Burchard making it five or six miles and another writer ten; and he notes that the place is the same as Kirjath-sepher and Kirjath-sannah, the city of a book or of books, that the Persian name is said to carry the same sense, and that it was so called from a library or from archives kept there.

Clarke agrees that Eglon cannot have been far from Lachish, and states the difficulty about Hebron without softening it: the earlier verses make the king of Hebron one of the five whom Joshua slew and hanged upon trees at Makkedah, so that it is hard to see how he can be said to slay the king of Hebron when he took the city some days afterwards; either the statement refers back to what had already been done, or else the Hebronites, finding that their king had fallen in battle, had set up another in his place, and it was this second king whom Joshua slew after the city was taken. Over the formula of utter destruction he alone hesitates, since the words mean that they brought every person under an anathema, and he asks whether it is not reasonable to hold that those found in arms were slain while of the others they made slaves. Wesley says that Eglon fell on the day they first attempted it, notices that the conquest of Hebron is related here only in general and is afterwards repeated and described more particularly, explains that the cities belonging to Hebron were those under its jurisdiction, it being a royal city like Gibeon with towns dependent on it, and takes the word return not as implying that Joshua had been at Debir before but as marking his turn back toward Gilgal, which lay north and east, after he had gone as far west and south as he thought fit, even as far as Gaza.

Keil and Delitzsch have Joshua proceeding eastwards from Lachish against Eglon, taking the town and doing to it as he had done to Lachish, then going up from the lowland to the mountains against Hebron and treating the town, its king and its dependent villages as the others had been treated, while adding at once that the king of Hebron here cannot be the man already executed at Makkedah; from Hebron he turns southwards with the whole army and takes Debir and the towns dependent upon it in the same manner, leaving none remaining, as he had done to Hebron and to Libnah before it. Ellicott says flatly that Debir has not been identified.

debates: Which king of Hebron was slain: Clarke poses the difficulty that the king of Hebron had already been hanged at Makkedah and offers two solutions, either a reference back to what was done there or the setting up of a successor whom Joshua killed when the city fell, while Keil and Delitzsch simply state that the king named here cannot be the one already executed

How far the ban extended: Clarke alone hesitates over the formula of utter destruction, suggesting that those found in arms were slain while the rest were reduced to slavery, where Gill and Keil and Delitzsch read a destruction that left none remaining
outliers: Gill derives the name of Debir from a library or archives kept in the place, noting that it was also called the city of a book or of books
Wesley explains the word return as marking the point at which Joshua, having reached as far as Gaza, turned back toward Gilgal and fell upon Debir on the way

40.pericope_label: The summary of the southern campaign and the return to Gilgal

schools.summary: Gill takes the summary for that part of Canaan which lay southward and consisted of hills and vales, a country abounding with springs and well watered, and observes that it answers the description Moses gave of it though he never saw it; he says the phrase about one time means not one day but a very short time, a few days, as the history clearly shows, and notes that the return took place only after all the kings and their cities had been taken, though the same words stood earlier in the chapter. Calvin sets out the whole ground of the defence: the divine authority is interposed again in order to acquit Joshua of any charge of cruelty, for had he proceeded of his own accord to an indiscriminate massacre of women and children no excuse could have cleared him of a detestable cruelty surpassing anything recorded of savage tribes scarcely raised above the level of the brutes; yet what would otherwise justly horrify us it becomes us to embrace with reverence as proceeding from God. Clemency, he adds, is rightly praised as one of the principal virtues, but it is the clemency of men who moderate their wrath when they have been injured and might with justice have shed blood; and since God had destined the swords of his people for the slaughter of the Amorites, Joshua could do nothing but obey the command.

Clarke reports that Calmet contends the Goshen named here was the very country in which the Hebrews dwelt before leaving Egypt and has drawn his map accordingly, extending it from the Nile along the frontiers of Cush, but thinks it plain that there was a city of that name in the tribe of Judah which probably gave its name to the neighbouring country. He narrows the destruction itself, holding that those destroyed were the persons found in arms who continued to resist, that those who submitted were spared, and that many no doubt escaped and afterwards reoccupied parts of the land; and on the one campaign he presses the inference that the conquests were so rapid and stupendous that they cannot be attributed either to Joshua’s generalship or to the valour of the Israelites, the author himself disclaiming the merit of them and modestly and piously adding that the Lord God of Israel fought for Israel, so that when all the circumstances are weighed both reason and piety require the whole to be ascribed to God alone. Wesley marks the limits of the expedition, Kadesh-barnea in the south and Gaza in the south-west, so that Joshua subdued all the parts lying south and west of Gilgal, and says shortly that the Goshen meant is not the Goshen of Egypt but another in Judah. He argues that the clause about the command is added for the vindication of the Israelites, whom God would not have suffer in their reputation for executing his orders, so that he acquits them of the cruelty they might be thought guilty of and takes it upon his own just indignation; and he reads the whole as a type of the final destruction of the impenitent enemies of the Lord Jesus, who, having slighted the riches of his grace, must for ever feel the weight of his wrath, adding that all that breathed means all mankind, the cattle being reserved for Israel’s own use.

Ellicott identifies the four regions in turn, the hills being the mountains of Judah and Ephraim, the south the Negeb, the vale the Shephelah or plain of the coast though apparently not taking in the Philistine territory which Joshua never conquered, and the springs a word which some render slopes or declivities, the country lying between the high hills and the low plain of the coast. Over Goshen he admits the difficulty and refuses the easy answer, since it is inconceivable that a single place of no importance in the mountains of Judah should have given its name to the extensive district manifestly intended here, and he would want to know the northern boundary of the Egyptian Goshen before deciding. He ends on the camp itself, a central position with Jordan and the conquered territory of the two and a half tribes lying in the rear. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the disputed word as once, that is in one campaign, which nevertheless lasted a considerable while, and add that Joshua was able to accomplish it because Jehovah the God of Israel fought for Israel, after which he returned with the army to the camp at Gilgal.

debates: What the country of Goshen means here: Wesley distinguishes it flatly from the Egyptian Goshen and finds another of the name in Judah, Clarke reports Calmet’s contrary identification with the land of the sojourn and prefers the Judahite town, while Ellicott holds it inconceivable that so unimportant a place should name a whole district and leaves the question open

How the destruction is to be judged: Calvin makes the express command of God the only thing that separates it from a cruelty surpassing that of savages, Wesley says the same and adds that God takes the act upon his own just indignation, while Clarke narrows the fact by holding that only those who continued in arms were destroyed and that many escaped to reoccupy the land
outliers: Gill notes that the description of the southern country answers what Moses had written of a land he never saw
Clarke refuses to credit the campaign either to Joshua’s generalship or to Israelite valour, and takes the writer’s own closing clause as a disclaimer of merit
Ellicott reads the choice of Gilgal as a strategic one, a central base with the river and the already conquered trans-Jordan behind it
